title: Design a Ticket Booking System
summary: Sell every seat for a concert or flight exactly once, even when thousands of people click "buy" on the same handful of good seats in the same second.

slides.markdown:
The ask: sell a fixed set of seats for an event without ever selling the same seat twice, even when an on-sale opens and thousands of requests hit the same few good seats in the same instant.

Think of it like a single stack of numbered tickets at a box-office window — only one clerk can hand out ticket #42, no matter how many people are shouting for it at once. Everything in this design exists to be that clerk: correct under contention, not just fast.

The hard part is never the seating-chart UI — it's making "one seat, one buyer" hold true under load.

**Functional:** search seats for an event, place a time-boxed **hold** on one, confirm the booking with payment, and release a hold that isn't confirmed in time.

**Non-functional:** zero tolerance for overselling a seat — that's the one guarantee that can never break, even during a traffic spike a hundred times normal. Hold duration is short (2-10 minutes) so abandoned carts free seats back up quickly rather than starving the on-sale.

**Explicit non-goal:** the seating-chart rendering and browsing UX. That's a front-end concern; the interesting system-design problem is what happens the instant two people click the same seat.

A popular stadium show might sell 50,000 seats. Steady-state that's nothing — but at 10:00:00am on-sale, 500,000 fans can hit refresh in the same second, all trying to grab one of the same few thousand "good" seats near the stage.

That's the number that matters: not seats-per-day, but **concurrent write attempts on the same narrow row of hot rows** in the first 5-10 seconds. If your hold-table can do 5,000 conditional writes/sec but 50,000 requests arrive in one second targeting a few hundred rows, the system doesn't fail from total load — it fails from **contention on a tiny hot set**.

Design for that spike, not for the daily average.

Four calls carry the whole flow:

- `searchSeats(eventId, filters)` — read-heavy, served from a cache or replica; staleness here is fine, it's just discovery.
- `holdSeat(seatId)` — the hot path: a conditional write that only succeeds if the seat is currently `available`.
- `confirmBooking(holdId, paymentToken)` — turns a hold into a sold seat once payment clears.
- `releaseHold(holdId)` — explicit release on cancel, plus an automatic expiry if the hold times out.

Notice `holdSeat` is the only call that needs to be airtight under concurrency — `searchSeats` can be sloppy-fast, `holdSeat` must be slow-but-correct if it has to be.

slides.sectionTitle: Data model: a seat-status table, not a counter
slides.markdown:
The tempting shortcut is a single `seatsAvailable` counter per event — fast to read, easy to decrement. It's also wrong: a counter can't tell you *which* seat was sold, so two buyers can both be told "you got a seat" while pointing at the same physical chair.

The correct model is one row per seat: `(eventId, seatId, status, holdId, holdExpiresAt)` with `status` in `available | held | sold`. Each `holdSeat` call is a conditional update — "set status='held' WHERE seatId=X AND status='available'" — so the database itself resolves the race: exactly one of two concurrent requests sees the update succeed.

The row is the unit of contention, and that's deliberate — it confines the race to one seat, not the whole event.

slides.sectionTitle: The core problem: two buyers, one seat
slides.markdown:
Strip away everything else and the system is one guarantee: if requests A and B both try to hold seat 14C at the same instant, exactly one succeeds and the other gets a clean "already taken" — never both succeeding, and never both failing.

This is a textbook **race condition**: read-then-write without atomicity lets both requests read `available`, then both write `held`. The fix is making the check-and-set a single atomic operation the database enforces, not two steps your application code performs separately.

Everything from here — locking strategy, queueing, holds — is in service of that one atomic operation.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: pessimistic locking vs optimistic concurrency
slides.markdown:
| | Pessimistic locking | Optimistic concurrency |
|---|---|---|
| How it works | `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` locks the row before reading | Read a version number, write with `WHERE version = X`, retry on mismatch |
| Under low contention | Pays lock overhead for no reason | Almost always succeeds first try — cheap |
| Under an on-sale spike | Requests queue behind the lock; predictable but can pile up | Most requests fail-and-retry on hot seats — cheap failures, but retry storms need backoff |
| Failure mode | A slow transaction holds the lock and stalls everyone behind it | A thundering herd of retries can itself become load |

**How to decide:** optimistic concurrency wins for ticket booking specifically because a "failed" hold attempt is cheap and informative (seat's gone, stop retrying) — you want fast-fail, not fast-queue, when 500 people want the same seat.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: two users racing for the same seat
slides.markdown:
![Two buyers racing to hold the same seat, only one write succeeds](assets/seat-race.svg)

Both requests race to the same row, but the database's conditional write is the single point where the tie is broken — only the request whose `WHERE status='available'` still matches at write time succeeds.

The loser doesn't get an error page — it gets an instant "that seat just went, here are similar ones," which is a better experience than a spinner that eventually times out.

slides.sectionTitle: Temporary holds: reserving without permanently locking
slides.markdown:
A **hold** is a seat marked `held` with a `holdExpiresAt` timestamp a few minutes out — long enough to enter payment details, short enough that an abandoned checkout doesn't starve the on-sale. It is not a database lock held open across a network round-trip to a payment provider; that would tie up a row (and a connection) for however long a slow card processor takes.

A background sweeper (or a check inline on the next `holdSeat` attempt) flips any `held` row whose `holdExpiresAt` has passed back to `available`. This turns "lock and wait" into "mark and expire" — the seat is protected during checkout but self-heals if the buyer walks away.

slides.sectionTitle: Handling the on-sale moment: queueing and virtual waiting rooms
slides.markdown:
When 500,000 people hit refresh at 10:00:00am, letting all of them straight through to `holdSeat` just moves the thundering herd from the front door to the database. A **virtual waiting room** admits users to the booking flow at a rate the backend can actually handle — everyone gets a queue position immediately, then is let in gradually.

This isn't about total throughput (the event only has 50,000 seats regardless); it's about **shaping the arrival curve** so the hot-row contention from earlier slides happens at a rate the seat-status table can resolve cleanly instead of falling over in the first second.

Critically, the waiting room sits in front of the system, admission-controlled — it's a pressure valve, not a workaround for a slow database.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: database-level locking vs a distributed lock service
slides.markdown:
| | Database-level locking | Distributed lock service (e.g. Redis, ZooKeeper) |
|---|---|---|
| Where the truth lives | The seat-status table itself is the lock | A separate service grants a lock token independent of the data store |
| Simplicity | One system to reason about and operate | Another moving part: its own availability and failure modes |
| Use case fit | Great when contention is scoped to rows in one datastore, as here | Better when a lock must span multiple services or datastores |
| Risk | None extra — the DB you already have is the source of truth | Lock can expire mid-operation, or the lock service itself can partition |

**How to decide:** for seat booking, the contention is entirely within one table, so a conditional write against the database *is* the lock — reaching for a separate lock service adds an operational dependency without buying correctness you didn't already have.

![End-to-end booking flow from search to confirmBooking, with hold expiry as the fallback path](assets/booking-flow.svg)

The flow has exactly one point of permanent commitment — `confirmBooking` succeeding — and everything before it is reversible by design, either explicitly (`releaseHold`) or by timeout.

That reversibility is what makes abandoned checkouts safe: a seat can be held, half-paid-for, and abandoned, and still end up back in inventory without anyone intervening.

assets.alt: End-to-end booking flow from search to confirmBooking, with hold expiry as the fallback path

slides.sectionTitle: The bottleneck: row-level contention at the on-sale instant
slides.markdown:
The system's real bottleneck isn't total throughput — it's the handful of best seats (front row, aisle) that a disproportionate share of the first second's traffic targets. Even with the waiting room shaping overall admission, those specific rows still see far more attempted writes than average.

Two mitigations compound: the admission-controlled queue from earlier caps how many requests reach the database per second at all, and optimistic concurrency (§7) makes each failed attempt on a hot row cheap — a fast "gone" rather than a slow queued wait. Neither alone is enough; together they turn a stampede into a manageable, if lumpy, write rate.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: releasing a hold only on success
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "I'll release the hold when the user cancels checkout — that covers it."

**Why it's wrong:** users close the tab, lose signal, or just walk away without clicking cancel. If release only happens on an explicit user action, every abandoned checkout permanently leaks a seat — over a busy on-sale day, that can be a meaningful fraction of total inventory quietly stuck in `held` forever.

**Correct model:** every hold gets a `holdExpiresAt` at creation time, and expiry is enforced independent of the client — a sweeper job or a check on next access reclaims it. Never rely on the client telling you it gave up.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: no idempotency key on confirmBooking
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Confirming a booking is a single call, so retries aren't a special case."

**Why it's wrong:** a client retry after a timeout — the request actually succeeded but the response was lost — will call `confirmBooking` again. Without protection, that can charge the card twice or, worse, try to sell an already-sold seat to the same buyer as a second booking.

**Correct model:** `confirmBooking` takes a client-generated **idempotency key**; the server stores the outcome of the first call keyed on it and replays that same result for any duplicate, rather than re-executing the charge. See [idempotency and exactly-once](idempotency-and-exactly-once) for the general pattern — this is one of its highest-stakes applications.

slides.sectionTitle: Summary: row-level state plus a time-boxed hold
slides.markdown:
Double-booking becomes impossible not through a clever algorithm but through two boring, disciplined choices: model inventory as one row per seat so a database write can atomically arbitrate contention, and bound every reservation with an expiry so abandoned checkouts self-heal instead of leaking seats.

Everything else — the waiting room, optimistic concurrency, idempotency keys — exists to make that core guarantee hold up under real-world load and real-world flaky clients, not to replace it. The same shape reappears in hotel booking with date ranges instead of single rows.
